title: Offering the Prize
coreMove: Present the offer as selective value and make the room qualify for fit instead of chasing its approval.
sourcePressure: Prizing chapter: the presenter protects value by avoiding needy seller energy, qualifying fit, and showing that the opportunity has selective value rather than begging for approval.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer must avoid turning prizing into false aloofness; the stance must come from real value, scarcity, and fit.

exampleSpecs.domain: specialty logistics firm offering limited cold-storage capacity to seafood exporters
exampleSpecs.audience: a logistics director who usually begs for volume commitments
exampleSpecs.stakes: the wrong customer fills scarce freezer slots and blocks higher-fit shipments
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: when the exporter asks for a discount, she points to the remaining pallet calendar and asks whether their harvest timing actually fits the open slots
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a freezer-slot calendar clipped to a clipboard with frost on the edge

exampleSpecs.domain: private aviation maintenance shop choosing which charter fleet to onboard
exampleSpecs.audience: a shop owner tempted to justify every premium labor rate
exampleSpecs.stakes: taking the wrong fleet crowds out existing aircraft and damages turnaround promises
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he stops defending the hourly rate and asks for the fleet's maintenance history before deciding whether the shop can take them
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a turbine blade inspection sheet beside a hangar key ring

exampleSpecs.domain: specialized language school pitching executive immersion seats to a diplomatic institute
exampleSpecs.audience: a program director whose limited cohort seats must feel selective for real reasons
exampleSpecs.stakes: the institute wants seats for unprepared candidates who would slow the cohort
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she slides the placement rubric forward and explains that the seat opens only if the candidate can sustain the second-week negotiation drill
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a placement rubric beside a stack of passport copies

exampleSpecs.domain: rare-instrument restorer discussing a violin repair with a touring soloist's manager
exampleSpecs.audience: an artisan whose scarcity is real but can sound arrogant if mishandled
exampleSpecs.stakes: accepting a rushed repair risks the instrument and the restorer's waiting list
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she sets the repair calendar between them and asks whether the tour schedule permits the curing time before quoting price
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a cracked violin rib under a bench lamp beside a linen repair calendar

exampleSpecs.domain: AI-chip allocation manager briefing robotics startups on a constrained pilot batch
exampleSpecs.audience: a technical business lead with more demand than supply
exampleSpecs.stakes: chips go to teams that cannot validate the batch while better-fit pilots wait
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after a chaotic meeting, he notes where he pitched availability instead of making each startup prove its test rig readiness
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a sealed antistatic chip tray beside a pilot-readiness checklist

exampleSpecs.domain: heritage seed cooperative selecting restaurant partners for a limited bean harvest
exampleSpecs.audience: a cooperative manager who must protect member growers from needy distribution deals
exampleSpecs.stakes: a chef treats the beans as garnish and wastes a crop that could build the cooperative's reputation
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she asks the chef to name the menu slot and purchase cadence before revealing how many sacks are available
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a cloth sack of speckled beans on a stainless prep counter

skillTargets: choose qualification questions tied to real scarcity
evaluate whether fit is substantive or performative

tryThisNowSpec: Write one real constraint that makes your offer selective, then turn it into a fit question you can ask before discussing terms.
